title: Blue Angels airshow crash
summary: During the final minutes of an airshow at Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort, Blue Angels aircraft number 6 crashed in a residential neighborhood. LCDR Kevin Davis, attempting to catch up to the lead aircraft with a faster and tighter turn than usual while performing a rendezvous maneuver, experienced a high-G turn (6.8 G) that subjected him to forces exceeding six times normal gravity. The rapid onset G forces and high turn rate caused spatial disorientation and tunnel vision, resulting in loss of altitude awareness. The aircraft struck terrain while in a steep right-wing-down bank at only 54 degrees, killing the pilot and injuring eight people on the ground.
probable_cause: LCDR Davis executed an excessively aggressive turn while attempting to catch up to the other aircraft during a rendezvous maneuver, subjecting himself to high-G forces (6.8 G) at rapid onset rate that caused spatial disorientation and loss of altitude awareness, resulting in loss of control and impact with terrain. (Command Investigation findings)

factors.evidence: LCDR Davis executed a sharper-than-usual right-hand 270-degree turn estimated at 6-7 G's out of the Loop Break Cross maneuver to cross above other aircraft; then performed a 'squatting' turn with rapid onset rate of at least 6.8 G in attempt to rendezvous with the lead aircraft (Delta); witnesses stated #6 was faster than usual and 'really squatted' the jet with a high G turn (Finding 75, 78, 81)

High-G maneuver with rapid onset (6.8 G) resulted in loss of blood flow to brain causing tunnel vision and disorientation; pilot failed to perform proper anti-G straining maneuver (AGSM) throughout the maneuver; pilot did not check in on radio at rendezvous point, indicating loss of situational awareness (Finding 78, 81-84)

After 'squatting the jet,' pilot maintained right-wing-down, slightly nose-low attitude until disappearing below tree line; pilot failed to monitor altitude during high-G turn and did not recover from spatial disorientation before impact (Finding 79)

Aircraft impacted in sparse residential area approximately 3 miles west of MCAS Beaufort; at impact, aircraft was in 6.8G, 54-degree right-wing-down roll, -1.4 degrees nose-down, at 320 knots with both engines at max afterburner; debris field approximately 2,000 feet long; pilot found without pulse strapped in ejection seat at far end of debris field (Finding 93, 94, 100, 107)

events.text: All six McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornets of the Blue Angels are making final turns into landing pattern during airshow at Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort; weather clear with few clouds at 5,000 feet, visibility unlimited, temperature 74°F, winds variable 3 knots (Finding 70)

Blue Angel #6 (LCDR Kevin Davis) executes sharper-than-usual right-hand 270-degree high-G turn estimated at 6-7 G's out of Loop Break Cross maneuver, crossing above #'s 4 and 5 to set up rendezvous (Finding 75)
LCDR Davis goes somewhat wings-level after high-G turn, maintaining level flight path while accelerating toward Delta (lead formation) for rendezvous (Finding 76-77)

LCDR Davis executes 'squatting of the jet' with rapid onset rate turn of at least 6.8 G in attempt to rendezvous with Delta formation; witnesses report #6 faster than normal and 'really squats' the jet with high G turn (Finding 78, 81)
LCDR Davis should check in on radio with callsign per SOP but only a mike click is heard; other pilots, unsure where #6 is, assume minor problem and continue performance (Finding 82-84)

Aircraft maintains right-wing-down, slightly nose-low attitude until disappearing below tree line; aircraft in 6.8G, 54-degree right-wing-down roll, -1.4 degrees nose-down pitch, 320 knots, both engines at maximum afterburner (Finding 79, 94)

Aircraft impacts terrain in sparse residential area approximately 3 miles west of MCAS Beaufort at coordinates N 32 26 89, W080 46 31; aircraft completely destroyed; debris field extends approximately 2,000 feet from first tree impact to final resting position (Finding 93, 100)

LCDR Davis found without pulse, face down, still strapped into ejection seat at far end of debris field; rescue personnel from MCAS Beaufort arrive within 3-4 minutes but pilot does not survive; multiple blunt force injuries determined as cause of death (Finding 107, 110, 115, 117)
Blue Angels #1 and #3 wave off their landings and head to crash site; #1 assumes on-scene commander duties; eight civilians on ground sustain injuries from debris impact (Finding 88-89)

recommendations.text: Implement focused research to develop appropriate G-suit for use by Naval Flight Demonstration Squadron pilots to enhance physiological tolerance to high-G maneuvers

Implement multi-day G tolerance optimization training program with CFET physiologist to improve G technique of each NFDS pilot; all new NFDS pilots to complete program in September 2007; entire team to attend refresher training October or November 2007
Flight Surgeon to develop weight training program targeting muscle groups needed to maximize G tolerance; program to be mandatory for all NFDS pilots
Make medical record entries for all military personnel who responded to or walked crash scene documenting potential exposure to crash debris (carbon fibers and hazardous materials) from F/A-18 crash

safety_changes: NFDS resumed flying practice flights on 30 April 2007 with G-suit waiver extension implemented
NFDS resumed airshow demonstrations in May 2007 following updated waiver by Chief of Naval Operations
Navy implemented new G-suit development program to provide enhanced physiological protection for demonstration pilots

notes: Deep read from JAG (Judge Advocate General) Manual Investigation Report for Naval Flight Demonstration Squadron mishap at MCAS Beaufort, South Carolina
9 events extracted from Findings of Fact sections detailing mishap sequence (Finding 75-94)
Military investigation report structure differs from civilian NTSB format; no formal probable cause statement but detailed findings establish causal factors
LCDR Kevin Davis (pilot) was sole occupant; 8 civilians on ground injured, none fatally
Investigation determined pilot did not perform proper anti-G straining maneuver (AGSM) during high-G turn, contributing to spatial disorientation
G-suit waiver had expired in 2004; not wearing G-suit did not contribute to mishap per investigation opinion
